body:
Why Plants Need to Transport Manufactured Food

Water and minerals are absorbed mainly by roots, but organic food is produced chiefly in photosynthetic tissues. Every living part of a plant requires a supply of energy and materials for growth and maintenance.

Roots, developing fruits, seeds and many growing tissues cannot always manufacture enough food for their own requirements. Carbohydrates produced in leaves therefore need to be transported to other parts of the plant.

This transport is carried out by the vascular tissue called phloem.

Translocation is the movement of soluble organic substances, especially products of photosynthesis, through phloem from regions supplying those substances to regions using or storing them.

What Does Phloem Transport?

Phloem transports soluble organic compounds, particularly sugars such as sucrose. It can also transport amino acids and other dissolved substances.

The destination depends on the needs of the plant. Manufactured food may be delivered to:

  • Roots: For respiration, growth and storage.
  • Developing fruits: For growth and accumulation of sugars or other organic substances.
  • Seeds: For the formation of stored food reserves.
  • Young shoots and buds: For active growth and development.
  • Storage organs: For accumulation of food that may be used later.

Structure of Phloem

Phloem contains conducting cells called sieve-tube elements. In flowering plants, these cells are associated with specialised companion cells that support their functioning.

Unlike mature xylem vessels and tracheids, sieve-tube elements are living conducting cells, although mature sieve-tube elements lack a nucleus and depend on associated companion cells for several metabolic functions.

How Food Moves Through Phloem

The movement of food in phloem can be understood through the relationship between sugar concentration, water movement and pressure.

  1. Sugar loading: Soluble sugars such as sucrose are transferred into phloem at a supplying region. In many plants, this loading involves energy derived from ATP.
  2. Water entry: The increased concentration of dissolved sugars causes water to enter phloem through osmosis.
  3. Pressure development: Water entry raises pressure in the phloem at the supplying region.
  4. Movement towards the receiving region: The pressure difference helps drive the movement of dissolved substances towards tissues where sugars are being used or stored.

This is a simplified description of pressure-driven phloem transport.

Phloem transport involves energy-dependent processes such as sugar loading. The subsequent mass movement of phloem sap is driven mainly by pressure differences.

Source and Sink

A source is a plant region that supplies more transported organic material than it uses. A mature photosynthesising leaf is a common source.

A sink is a region that receives transported organic material because it needs the material for growth, respiration or storage. Developing fruits and growing roots are examples.

The source and sink roles can change with the plant's stage of growth. For example, a storage organ may act as a sink while reserves accumulate and later act as a source when stored carbohydrates are mobilised to growing shoots.

Consequently, phloem transport is not restricted to movement from top to bottom. Food may travel upward or downward according to the locations of sources and sinks. Within an individual conducting pathway, the bulk movement is normally in one direction at a given time.

Xylem and Phloem Compared

FeatureXylemPhloem
Main transported substancesWater and dissolved mineral nutrientsSugars and other soluble organic compounds
Common routeRoots towards leaves and other aerial tissuesSources towards sinks
DirectionMainly upward in transpiring plantsUpward or downward, according to plant needs
Principal conducting structuresVessels and tracheidsSieve-tube elements with companion cells
Driving processesMainly transpiration pull, with contribution from root pressurePressure differences supported by sugar loading and unloading
Energy useWater flow is largely passiveLoading and unloading can require metabolic energy

How the Processes Work Together

The major plant life processes are closely linked.

Roots absorb water and dissolved mineral nutrients from the soil. Xylem carries much of this water upward to leaves. Stomata admit carbon dioxide, while chlorophyll-containing cells use light energy to manufacture carbohydrates.

Some water is lost from leaves through transpiration, which helps pull additional water through xylem. Phloem distributes soluble products of photosynthesis to growing and storage tissues. Those tissues use or store the transported compounds.

Thus, photosynthesis, transpiration and internal transportation form a connected system that supports the survival and growth of the plant.

Simple Applications

A Growing Fruit

A developing fruit may accumulate sugars even though much of its food was originally manufactured in leaves. Phloem carries these organic substances from photosynthetic sources to the developing fruit.

A Plant Experiencing Water Shortage

When root absorption cannot replace water lost through transpiration, guard cells may lose turgor and stomata may close. This conserves water but also reduces carbon dioxide entry, potentially lowering photosynthesis.

A Tree with Damaged Phloem

Damage to phloem can interrupt the supply of manufactured food to tissues beyond the damaged region. This can impair growth or survival even if xylem water transport remains partly functional.

Roots and leaves are connected by both xylem and phloem, but these tissues transport different principal substances. Water transport and food translocation must not be treated as the same process.

Integrated Revision

The complete relationship can be understood as a sequence of material supply, food production and distribution.

  • Roots: Absorb water and minerals.
  • Xylem: Carries water and dissolved minerals, mainly upward.
  • Stomata: Permit gas exchange and regulate much of the water-vapour loss.
  • Chloroplasts: Use captured light energy to manufacture carbohydrates from carbon dioxide and water.
  • Transpiration: Helps generate the pull that moves water through xylem.
  • Phloem: Distributes soluble organic food from sources to sinks.

Prelims focus

  • Xylem transports water and dissolved minerals.
  • Phloem transports soluble products of photosynthesis.
  • Translocation is the movement of organic substances through phloem.
  • Sieve-tube elements and companion cells participate in phloem transport.
  • Phloem transport can occur upward or downward according to source-sink relationships.
  • Trap: Phloem is not restricted to downward food movement, and xylem is not the principal tissue for transporting manufactured sugars.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 5, Life Processes, Section 5.4.2, Transportation in Plants, printed pp. 94–96, reprint 2026–27; GCERT, Science, Std. 10, Chapter 5, Life Processes, Section 5.4.2, printed pp. 94–96; NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 11, Transportation in Animals and Plants, Section 11.3, printed pp. 128–131, 2018–19 reprint; NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 6, Tissues, Section 6.2.2, plant conducting tissues; OpenStax, Biology 2e, Section 30.5, Transport of Water and Solutes in Plants, consulted 4 November 2026.]

title: Phloem Translocation and the Coordination of Plant Life Processes
